nameStory: Common cottongrass gets its name from the fluffy white seed heads that look exactly like cotton balls dancing in the wind. After the small, unremarkable flowers are pollinated in early summer, they transform into these distinctive white bristle-like tufts that can be spotted from quite a distance across wetlands.
description: Common cottongrass is a hardy perennial sedge that forms colonies in boggy areas through underground stems called rhizomes. It grows about 1-2 feet tall with narrow, grass-like leaves and produces small brownish-green flowers in spring. The real showstopper comes later when those flowers develop into brilliant white, cottony seed heads that wave in the breeze like tiny flags across the wetland.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Bright white, fluffy cotton-ball tufts on tall stems that catch the slightest breeze and practically glow against dark bog backgrounds - unmistakable once you see them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that feel slightly rough to the touch and emerge directly from the base, typically dark green and about 1/8 inch wide

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, clustered brownish-green flowers that appear unremarkable in late spring - you might walk right past them before they transform into the showy seed heads

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms colonies through underground rhizomes, creating patches of identical plants that sway together in unison across wet areas

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Triangular in cross-section when you roll them between your fingers - a classic sedge trait that separates them from round-stemmed grasses

habitat: Look for common cottongrass in acidic, peaty wetlands like bogs, fens, and soggy meadows throughout New England's higher elevations and northern regions. It thrives in permanently wet, nutrient-poor soils where few other plants can compete, often growing alongside sphagnum moss, pitcher plants, and other bog specialists.

seasonality.spring: Small brownish-green flower clusters appear in April or May, easily overlooked among the emerging green leaves.
seasonality.summer: The magic happens in early to mid-summer when flowers transform into spectacular white cotton-ball seed heads that dominate the bog landscape.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads gradually break apart and disperse, leaving behind the persistent triangular stems and dying foliage.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and leaf bases remain visible above snow, creating golden-brown stubble patterns across frozen wetlands.

funFact: Indigenous peoples of North America discovered that cottongrass seeds are not only edible but quite nutritious - they can be eaten raw, cooked into porridge, or even ground into flour, making this bog plant an unexpected wilderness survival food.
confusionNotes: Despite the name, cottongrass isn't actually grass at all - it's a sedge! Remember the old botanist's rhyme: 'Sedges have edges' - roll the stem between your fingers and you'll feel the triangular shape that grasses never have.
contextualKnowledge: Don't expect to make clothing from cottongrass despite its cotton-like appearance - the fibers are too short and weak for textiles. However, resourceful Northern Europeans historically used these fluffy seed heads to stuff pillows, make paper, create candle wicks, and even dress wounds.
compareHints: Common cottongrass typically has multiple nodding seed heads per stem, while tussock cottongrass usually has just one erect cottony head per stem. Tawny cottongrass produces rusty-brown rather than bright white seed heads, making it easy to distinguish once the fluffy stage arrives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cottongrasses, tawny cottongrass is unique for its brown seed heads - common cottongrass and tussock cottongrass both have white or cream-colored fluff.
Tussock cottongrass is the only cottongrass that grows in distinctive single tussocks and produces just one seed head per stem.
Among New England's cottongrasses, green-keeled stands out with its bright white seed heads and prominently ridged leaves.
Rough cottongrass is the smallest and most delicate of New England's cottongrasses.
Among New England's cottongrasses, slender cottongrass stands out for its thin, delicate build and preference for the wettest bog conditions.
